About: the lighthouse model of a pulsar: steady beams carried round by the rotation

About this simulation

On screen
Top: the neutron star in 3D, drawn greatly enlarged, with the vertical rotation axis (Ω), the dashed magnetic axis at α, dipole field loops, two light-blue beam cones of half-width ρ, the faint trail of sky the beams have swept, and the 'to Earth' arrow at ζ, which lights up while the line of sight is inside a beam. Bottom: the radio flux received at the Earth, as a fraction of the flux inside a beam, against time from 0 to 8 s.
Controls
α sets the tilt of the magnetic axis from the rotation axis, ζ the angle of the line of sight from the rotation axis, ρ the half-width of each beam. Moving any of them clears the trace and the trail but keeps the star's rotation phase. ▶ Play starts or pauses the rotation at its true rate, once every 1.34 s. Drag the scene to turn the view.
Readouts
In the sidebar: ψ, the angle between the line of sight and the nearer beam axis at this moment; the closest each beam axis comes to the line of sight in a turn, |ζ − α| and |180° − ζ − α|; the number of pulses per turn and their length, once a full turn has been traced; and the fraction of all directions from which a beam is ever seen, summed over viewing angles on a 0.01° grid (2 sin α sin ρ when the two swept bands do not overlap).
Model
The lighthouse model: two steady beams along the magnetic axis, carried round by the rotation, with cos ψ = cos α cos ζ + sin α sin ζ cos φ at rotation phase φ. Each beam is a uniform cone with a sharp edge, so the flux is either full or zero. Real radio beams fade towards their edges, and for a 1.34 s pulsar they are only about 5° wide, narrower than the slider allows.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Watching the flux

Set α = 30°, ζ = 40° and ρ = 15°. Before pressing play, predict what the trace of the flux received at the Earth will show.

2 · Moving the Earth's view

Keep α = 30° and ρ = 15°. Before moving ζ from 40° to 70°, predict what the trace will show.

3 · Tilting the magnetic axis

Keep ζ = 70°, ρ = 15° and α = 30°. Before moving α, predict which of these inclinations brings the pulses back.

4 · Looking down the spin axis

Set α = 10°, ρ = 15° and ζ = 0°, so that the Earth lies on the rotation axis. Before pressing play, predict what the trace will show.

5 · Beams near the equator

Set α = 80°, ζ = 90° and ρ = 15°. Before pressing play, predict how many pulses arrive in each rotation of 1.34 s.

6 · How much sky the beams reach

Keep α = 80° and ρ = 15°, and note the fraction of the sky that the beams reach. Before setting α to 30°, predict how that fraction changes.

7 · What the lighthouse model says

The beams are steady; the pulses come from the rotation carrying them across our line of sight. We see beam 1 only if the line of sight passes within ρ of its axis, |ζ − α| < ρ (for beam 2, |180° − ζ − α| < ρ).

So one star can look pulsed once or twice per turn, steady, or dark, depending only on where we stand. The beams reach only bands covering about 2 sin α sin ρ of the sky, so we miss many pulsars.

In this model the beams are sharp-edged, uniform cones. Real radio beams fade towards their edges, and for a star turning once every 1.34 s they are only a few degrees wide.

The Lighthouse Model of a Pulsar

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A neutron star radiates two steady beams along its magnetic axis, and the rotation carries them round. This sim turns the star once every 1.34 s and records the flux that reaches the Earth, for any tilt of the magnetic axis, viewing angle and beam width.

What you'll learn

  • How the angle between the line of sight and a beam changes as the star turns.
  • What decides whether an observer ever sees a beam.
  • How the pulses in one turn are counted.
  • How much of the sky the beams reach.
The apparatus at the opening values: the star turns about Ω and carries both beams round.

What's on screen

  • White vertical line Ω: the rotation axis. The to Earth arrow is the line of sight, at angle ζ from it.
  • Dashed violet line: the magnetic axis, at angle α from Ω, with dipole field loops around the star.
  • Blue cones: beam 1 and beam 2, each of half-width ρ. A faint trail marks the sky they have swept.
  • Flux trace (lower panel): the flux at the Earth, as a fraction of the flux inside a beam, against time from 0 to 8 s. The Readouts panel gives ψ, the closest approaches, the pulse count and length, and the sky swept.
See itWatch the star turn at the opening values. Watch for: the star turning once every 1.34 s, carrying both beams round the vertical axis.

03

Full inside a beam, zero outside: the angle ψ decides

At each moment the line of sight makes an angle ψ with the axis of beam 1. A beam is a uniform cone of half-width ρ, so the flux is full while ψ < ρ and zero while ψ > ρ. As the star turns through the phase φ, the spherical law of cosines gives ψ (the sim's own model):

cos ψ = cos α cos ζ + sin α sin ζ cos φ

Angle ψ between the line of sight and beam 1; the beam is seen while ψ < ρ.

Beam 2 sits on the opposite axis, so ψ2 = 180° − ψ. At φ = 0, ψ is smallest, |ζ − α|. Half a turn later it is largest, α + ζ (when α + ζ ≤ 180°). So ψ swings once a turn between those two values. If ρ lies between them, a beam crosses the line of sight once each turn. In the notes' words, the interval between pulses is the spin period Ps.

Opening values: ψ (blue) dips below ρ (dashed) for part of the turn, and the flux (below) is full for exactly that part.

At the opening values ψ runs from 10° to 70° and is below ρ = 15° for about 40° of each 360° turn: a pulse about 0.15 s long, once every 1.34 s.

Key idea. In this model the flux between pulses is zero, not low: the Earth is inside a cone or it is not.
See itPlay the opening values. Watch for: a flat-topped pulse about 0.15 s long once every 1.34 s, with Earth inside a beam? reading yes during it.
04

Seen only if a beam passes within ρ: |ζ − α| < ρ

Over a turn, beam 1 comes as near as |ζ − α| to the line of sight, and beam 2 as near as |180° − ζ − α|. These are the two Closest approach in a turn rows in the Readouts. A beam is ever seen only if its closest approach is below ρ. Each beam therefore sweeps a band of viewing angles 2ρ wide.

Bands of viewing angle ζ from which each beam is seen at α = 30°, ρ = 15°.

At the opening values the closest approaches are 10° and 110°. Move ζ to 70° and they become 40° and 80°, both outside ρ = 15°: the star shines as before, but this observer sees no pulsar. Raise α to 60° (at ζ = 70°) and beam 1 comes within 10° again; any α between 55° and 85° does.

α ζ ρ

These sliders move the sim too. The result comes from the sim's own model.

See itMove the Earth to ζ = 70° (α = 30°, ρ = 15°). Watch for: a trace flat at 0 and Earth inside a beam? staying no, though the beams still sweep round.
See itNow tilt the magnetic axis to α = 60° (ζ = 70°). Watch for: the pulses coming back, with Beam 1, |ζ − α| reading 10°.
05

Down the spin axis the flux never changes

Rotation changes ψ only if the line of sight is off the axis. At ζ = 0° the Earth lies on Ω, and cos ψ = cos α for every φ: ψ = α all the way round, however fast the star turns.

So there are two cases. If α < ρ, the Earth sits inside beam 1 all the time and receives a steady flux, with no pulses. If α > ρ, it is never inside a beam and receives nothing. More generally the flux is steady whenever ψ stays below ρ through the whole turn, that is α + ζ < ρ for beam 1.

Key idea. A steady flux still means the Earth is inside a beam. Pulses need ψ to cross ρ, and that needs the line of sight off the rotation axis.
See itLook down the spin axis: α = 10°, ζ = 0°, ρ = 15°. Watch for: a trace flat at 1.0, Earth inside a beam? staying yes and ψ staying at 10.0° while the star turns.
06

Near the equator both beams pulse, half a turn apart

Beam 2 is the opposite axis, so it can also cross the line of sight. Both beams are seen when both closest approaches are below ρ. At α = 80°, ζ = 90° and ρ = 15° each is 10° away, so beam 1 and beam 2 pulse in turn: two pulses a turn, half a turn apart.

Flux over one turn at α = 80°, ζ = 90°, ρ = 15°: one pulse from each beam.

The pulses are 0.67 s apart, half of Ps = 1.34 s, and each is about 0.08 s long. An observer who only timed the pulses would take the period to be 0.67 s, half its true value. The flat tops come from the model's sharp-edged cones; the notes draw beams whose intensity falls off with angle from the axis.

See itSet α = 80°, ζ = 90°, ρ = 15° and play. Watch for: two flat pulses in each 1.34 s turn, 0.67 s apart, with Pulses per turn reading 2.
07

How much sky the beams reach: 2 sin α sin ρ

A beam is seen from every ζ in its band. The share of all directions between ζ = α − ρ and ζ = α + ρ is ½[cos(α − ρ) − cos(α + ρ)] = sin α sin ρ. Two separate bands give:

sky fraction = 2 sin α sin ρ

Fraction of the sky from which a beam is ever seen, for separate bands.

This holds for ρ ≤ α ≤ 90° − ρ, where the bands neither overlap nor reach a pole. At α = 30°, ρ = 15° it gives 0.26, about a quarter of the sky. Tilt to α = 80° and the bands overlap, so the sim's sum over viewing angles gives 0.42, less than the formula's 0.51. At α = 90° the bands coincide and the fraction falls back to 0.26.

Every other observer never sees this star pulse. The notes make the same point: only a fraction of the neutron stars in the Galaxy can be seen as pulsars.

See itTilt to α = 80° (ρ = 15°). Watch for: Sky swept by the beams reading 0.42.
See itNow lower α to 30°. Watch for: Sky swept by the beams falling to 0.26.
08

Where it matters

  • Counting pulsars. Only observers inside a band see a beam, so the pulsars we detect are only a fraction of the neutron stars that exist.
  • Reading the period. One crossing per turn gives pulse spacing Ps. If both beams cross the line of sight, the spacing is Ps/2.
  • Where the model stops. Real beams fade towards their edges, and for a 1.34 s pulsar they are only about 5° wide, narrower than the ρ slider allows.
09

Summary

In one line. Two steady beams turn with the star, and what reaches the Earth is set by the angle ψ between the line of sight and each beam axis, compared with the half-width ρ.

Common mix-ups

  • "The star itself turns on and off." The beams are steady; rotation carries them across the line of sight.
  • "Moving the Earth only makes the pulses weaker." In this model the Earth is inside a cone or not. At ζ = 70° (α = 30°, ρ = 15°) the flux is zero, not faint.
  • "A lighthouse always flashes once per turn." Two beams can give two pulses, and a view down the spin axis gives a steady flux or none.

Things to try on your own

  • At α = 30° and ρ = 15°, slide ζ from 0° to 180° and note where the pulses stop and restart. Compare with α ± ρ and 180° − α ± ρ.
  • Set ρ = 5° at α = 30°, ζ = 40°. Find the smallest and largest ζ that still give a pulse.
